finding.claim: NaN or -Infinity amounts corrupt balances. A NaN amount makes every later balance check pass, allowing unlimited spending. -Infinity in /transfer sets the sender balance to +inf and the victim balance to -inf.
finding.source: request.json["amount"] (bank.py:20 for withdraw, bank.py:10 for transfer); Flask's default json.loads accepts NaN, Infinity and -Infinity
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:23 for withdraw, bank.py:13 for transfer) and BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14)

trace.note: amount = NaN parsed from JSON body
NaN <= 0 is false and BAL[g.user] < NaN is false, so the check passes
later calls: NaN < amount is always false, so every subsequent withdrawal passes the check regardless of balance

finding.guards_checked: no math.isfinite or isinstance(int) validation on amount in either route; the amount<=0 check at bank.py:21 does not catch NaN

verdict.reason: The trace lines match bank.py:10, 13, 14, 20, 21, and 23; Python's json.loads (used by Flask's request.json) accepts NaN and Infinity, so at bank.py:21 `NaN <= 0` and `BAL < NaN` are both False and the withdraw proceeds, setting BAL[g.user] to NaN, after which every later `BAL < amount` comparison is False and the balance check no longer limits spending. The attacker needs only the authenticated user context that g.user already implies (g.user is set outside this file, so the auth model is UNVERIFIED, but it is not a role that already holds this power). The -Infinity transfer path (bank.py:11, 13, 14) also checks out.

finding.claim: /transfer debits the sender before validating the recipient. An unknown or unhashable 'to' raises after the debit, so the funds are destroyed and never rolled back.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:13) runs before BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14), which raises KeyError or TypeError

finding.guards_checked: no existence check on 'to'; no transaction or rollback; impact is self-inflicted loss rather than theft

finding.claim: Check-then-act race: concurrent /transfer or /withdraw requests by the same user can both pass the balance check before either debit, allowing overdraft and double spending. Plausible, not confirmed by a test.
finding.source: concurrent HTTP requests by the same authenticated user
finding.sink: unguarded read-check-write on BAL[g.user] (bank.py:11-13 and bank.py:21-23)

trace.note: request A reads balance and passes the check
request B reads the same balance before A writes and also passes
both debit, so balance goes negative or the money is spent twice
